citations.quote: Let $M\in D^-(\mathcal A)$ and $N\in D^+(\mathcal A)$, with termwise bounded representatives. With supplied bounded-above projective models under [[thm-projective-complexes-model-the-bounded-above-derived-category]], define $\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)=Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_M,N)$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. A **cochain complex in $\mathcal A$** is a family of objects $(C^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ together with morphisms $$d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$$ such that $$d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. We use cochains as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], with $X[k]^n=X^{n+k}$ and $d_{X[k]}^n=(-1)^kd_X^{n+k}$. Thus $H^n(X[k])=H^{n+k}(X)$. The cochain category $K(\mathcal A)$ is the reindexed published homotopy category.

derivations.claim: Kernels, images and cokernels of morphisms of diagrams of $k$-vector spaces are formed objectwise, so a morphism of diagrams is an epimorphism exactly when it is surjective at every object, and a complex of diagrams is exact exactly when it is exact at every object. In particular exactness questions about $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ reduce to the vector spaces $N(p)$, and no diagram-level machinery beyond the objectwise one is used below.

For $p\in P$ define the diagram $Q_p$ by $Q_p(q)=k$ for $p\le q$ and $Q_p(q)=0$ otherwise, with the identity as structure map whenever both values are nonzero. A natural transformation $\varphi:Q_p\to N$ is determined by $\varphi_p(1)\in N(p)$, since for $q\ge p$ the component $\varphi_q$ must equal $N(p\to q)\circ\varphi_p$ and for $q\ngeq p$ the source $Q_p(q)$ is zero; conversely every vector $v\in N(p)$ extends by these formulas. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_p,N)\cong N(p)$ by evaluation at $p$. Pulling back along the identification, a surjection $\pi:N\to N'$ induces the surjection $N(p)\to N'(p)$ by step 1.1, so every map $Q_p\to N'$ lifts to $N$ and $Q_p$ is projective. For a finite-dimensional $V$, a natural transformation $Q_p\otimes_kV\to N$ is likewise determined by its value at $p$, a $k$-linear map $V\to N(p)$, and conversely every such map extends uniquely by the structure maps of $N$, so $\operatorname{Hom}(Q_p\otimes_kV,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,N(p))$; since $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,-)$ carries surjections to surjections — lift the images of a finite basis and extend linearly — the diagram $Q_p\otimes_kV$ is projective as well. A finite direct sum of projectives is projective, because $\operatorname{Hom}(\bigoplus_tX_t,N)\cong\prod_t\operatorname{Hom}(X_t,N)$ and a finite product of surjections of vector spaces is surjective by induction on the number of factors. Only finitely many basis vectors and summands occur at each step, so no choice principle is used.

For a diagram $N$ put $\mathcal B_n(N)=\bigoplus_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}Q_{p_n}\otimes_kN(p_0)$ for $n\ge0$, with the face maps $\partial_i:\mathcal B_n(N)\to\mathcal B_{n-1}(N)$ ($n\ge1$, $0\le i\le n$) given on the summand of the chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n$ by: for $i=0$ apply the structure map $N(p_0)\to N(p_1)$ and delete $p_0$; for $0<i<n$ delete the inner vertex $p_i$, keeping the coefficient in $N(p_0)$ and the representable index $p_n$; for $i=n$ delete $p_n$ and use the natural map $Q_{p_n}\to Q_{p_{n-1}}$ (the identity where the source is $k$, and zero otherwise) while keeping the coefficient. Let $\partial=\sum_i(-1)^i\partial_i$ for $n\ge1$ and set $\partial=0$ in bar degree zero, before adjoining the augmentation. The simplicial identities $\partial_i\partial_j=\partial_{j-1}\partial_i$ for $i<j$ hold because diagram transport $p\mapsto N(p)$ is functorial and the maps between representables compose, so $\partial^2=0$; this is a sign-alternating sum of a simplicial identity. Since chains of $P$ have at most $h$ strict inequalities, $\mathcal B_n(N)=0$ for $n>h$. Augment by the structure maps $\epsilon:\mathcal B_0(N)\to N$, $Q_p\otimes_kN(p)\to N$, which are natural.

Evaluate the augmented complex at $q\in P$. Its degree-$n$ part consists of the chains $p_0<\cdots<p_n\le q$ with a vector of $N(p_0)$, the faces delete a vertex as in step 3.1, the last face being free to delete $q$, and the augmentation sends a length-zero chain $(p_0)$ to $N(p_0\to q)v$. Define a degree-$(-1)$-to-$0$ map $s_{-1}:N(q)\to\mathcal B_0(N)(q)$ by $v\mapsto(q,v)$, and for $n\ge0$ a degree-$n$-to-$n+1$ map $s_n$ on the summand of the chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n\le q$ by $s_n(v)=(-1)^{n+1}(p_0<\cdots<p_n<q,\,v)$ when $p_n<q$, and $s_n=0$ when $p_n=q$. One checks $\partial s_n+s_{n-1}\partial=\mathrm{id}$ on each evaluated component: the appended simplex contributes through its last face with sign $(-1)^{n+1}\cdot(-1)^{n+1}=1$, every other face is matched by the corresponding appended term in $s\partial$ with opposite sign, and in degree zero the augmentation section cancels exactly the last-face term; when $p_n=q$ and $n\ge1$, only the last face contributes to $s_{n-1}\partial$, with coefficient $(-1)^n(-1)^n=1$, while for $n=0$ the term $s_{-1}\epsilon$ is the identity. Moreover $\epsilon$ is surjective on the evaluated complexes because $(q,v)\mapsto v$, so the augmented evaluated complex is exact in every degree. Exactness is objectwise by step 1.1, so $\epsilon:\mathcal B(N)\to N$ is a quasi-isomorphism; and if every $N(p)$ is finite-dimensional then every $\mathcal B_n(N)$ is a finite direct sum of projectives by step 2.1, so $\mathcal B(N)$ is a bounded projective resolution of $N$.

Let $A$ be a bounded complex of diagrams with finite-dimensional values, vanishing outside internal degrees $[a,b]$, with internal differentials $d_A$. Apply the bar construction of step 4.1 to each internal degree $u$, so $\mathcal B_n(A^u)$ has bar degree $n\in[0,h]$ and carries the internal differential $d_A:\mathcal B_n(A^u)\to\mathcal B_n(A^{u+1})$. The face maps $\partial$ commute with the maps induced by $d_A$, since they are built from the structure maps of the diagrams and from the fixed maps between representables. Take the total complex $\operatorname{Tot}$ with $\operatorname{Tot}^m=\bigoplus_{u-n=m}\mathcal B_n(A^u)$ and differential $D=d_A+(-1)^u\partial$ on the summand $\mathcal B_n(A^u)$; the sign $(-1)^u$ makes the horizontal and vertical parts anticommute, so $D^2=0$. Each column $u$ maps quasi-isomorphically to $A^u$ by step 4.1, so the rows of the mapping cone of $\operatorname{Tot}\to A$ are the mapping cones of the augmentations $\mathcal B(A^u)\to A^u$ and are acyclic; a bounded double complex with acyclic rows has acyclic total complex, by filtering by the finitely many internal degrees and inducting on the number of rows with the long exact homology sequence of the quotient by the top row. Hence $\operatorname{Tot}\to A$ is a quasi-isomorphism, $\operatorname{Tot}$ is a complex of finite-dimensional projective diagrams by steps 2.1 and 4.1, and its total degrees $u-n$ lie in $[a-h,b]$.

Resolve the constant diagram $\underline k$ by its bar complex $\mathcal B(\underline k)$, a bounded complex of finite-dimensional projective diagrams of the form of step 4.1 with $\underline k$ in internal degree $0$. These bounded projective models require no DC: Hom from a single projective into an acyclic complex is acyclic by exactness of its Hom functor; filtering a bounded projective complex by its finitely many degrees and applying the cohomology sequence to the resulting termwise split Hom sequences proves the same for that complex. Hence Hom from the model preserves quasi-isomorphisms and computes [F1] without any infinite sequence of lifts. Then $\mathbf R\lim M=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,M)$ is computed by the Hom complex $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(\mathcal B(\underline k),M)$ of [F1], whose degree-$r$ term is $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal B(\underline k)^i,M^{i+r})$. Here $\mathcal B(\underline k)^{-n}=\bigoplus_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}Q_{p_n}$ is nonzero only for $0\le n\le h$ and $M^j=0$ for $j\notin[a,b]$, so by the vanishing rule of [F1] nonzero factors require $a-r\le i\le b$ with $-h\le i\le0$, so any nonzero factor has $r\in[a,b+h]$. Concretely the bar-degree-$n$ part is the finite product $\prod_{p_0<\cdots<p_n}M(p_n)$, so every term is a finite product of finite-dimensional spaces, hence finite-dimensional. Thus $\mathbf R\lim M$ has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[a,b+h]$.

For the pair $A,B$ concentrated in $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$, resolve the source by the total bar model $P_A:=\operatorname{Tot}$ of step 5.1, concentrated in $[a-h,b]$, and apply [F1]: $\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(A,B)$ is computed by $Q\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P_A,B)$, whose degree-$r$ term is the finite product $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(P_A^i,B^{i+r})$. A nonzero factor requires $P_A^i
e0$ and $B^{i+r}
e0$, hence $a-h\le i\le b$ and $c\le i+r\le d$; so for $r<c-b$ every $i$ with $P_A^i
e0$ has $i+r\le b+r<c$ and for $r>d-a+h$ every such $i$ has $i+r>d$, and in both cases every factor of the term vanishes. Thus the model is concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$. By the evaluation identity in step 2.1, each summand with $u-n=i$ and chain $p_0<\cdots<p_n$ contributes $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^u(p_0),B^{i+r}(p_n))$. Thus every term is a finite product of Hom spaces between finite-dimensional vector spaces, hence finite-dimensional.

Let $K/k$ be a field extension, and write the base-changed inputs as $K\otimes_kM$, $K\otimes_kA$, $K\otimes_kB$, diagrams over $K$. The models built in steps 5.2 and 6.1 have terms obtained from the values $M(p)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_k(A(p),B(q))$ by finite sums, finite products and the fixed face and structure maps; extending scalars commutes with finite direct sums, with finite products and, between finite-dimensional spaces, with Hom spaces, so $K\otimes_k$ of the model for $(M,A,B)$ is the model for the base-changed inputs, with the same signs and differentials. Tensoring with $K$ preserves kernels and images of linear maps between finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and hence commutes with the homology of a bounded complex of such spaces, so the cohomology of the base-changed model is the base change of the cohomology of the original model. This proves both base-change assertions. For the empty poset there are no chains, the diagram sections and the Hom complex vanish by the same product formulas, and the asserted model is zero.

The inclusion $C_\bullet^{\mathcal U}(X;G)\hookrightarrow C_\bullet(X;G)$ induces an isomorphism on homology.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be abelian categories, let $I$ be supplied

admit connecting maps that make them into a cohomological delta functor on
$\mathcal A$, and $R_I^0F$ is naturally isomorphic to $F$.

$$0\to A^\bullet\to B^\bullet\to C^\bullet\to0$$

derivations.claim: (Flasque sheaves are acyclic.) For an injective $k$-sheaf $I$, the monomorphism $j_{U!}k_U\to j_{V!}k_V$ for opens $U\subseteq V$ is the identity on stalks in $U$ and has zero source elsewhere. The adjunction [F10], restricted to $k$-linear maps, identifies Hom from these sheaves with $I(U)$ and $I(V)$: a map from $k_U$ is determined by its value on $1$, and locally constant scalar multiples are defined by gluing. Thus injectivity makes $I(V)\to I(U)$ onto, so $I$ is flasque. Embed a flasque $F$ into an injective $I$ using [F7], with quotient $Q$. By [F8], $I(U)\to Q(U)$ is onto and $Q$ is flasque. The long exact sequence and injective acyclicity [F11] give $H^1(X,F)=0$ and $H^{n+1}(X,F)\cong H^n(X,Q)$ for $n\ge1$. Induction, uniformly over flasque sheaves, proves their acyclicity. The same proof on any open subspace gives the assertion there. Repeating the argument for abelian sheaves, with $\mathbb Z_U$ in place of $k_U$ and [F14] for the injective data, proves abelian flasque acyclicity as well. No $k$-injective is claimed to be injective among abelian sheaves.

(Global representatives.) Let $C^n(U;k)$ be the functions on singular $n$-simplices with image in $U$, with the usual cochain differential, and let $\mathcal C^n$ be its sheafification. Locally represent $s\in\mathcal C^n(U)$ by cochains on an open cover $\{U_j\}$; local representability follows from the stalk bijection [F6]. The open subspace $U$ is itself metric, hence paracompact and Hausdorff by [F1], [F2]. Apply [F3] in $U$ to obtain a locally finite open cover $\{W_i\}$ and assigned indices $j(i)$ with $\overline{W_i}^{\,U}\subseteq U_{j(i)}$, and write $c_i$ for the representative on $U_{j(i)}$. For each singular simplex in $X$ whose image lies in some $W_i$, choose one such index and assign the value $c_i(\sigma)$; assign zero when no such index exists. These choices use [A1] and define a global cochain $c\in C^n(X;k)$. The germ verification below shows that its sheafification restricts to $s$.

(Prescribed germs and flasqueness.) Fix $x\in U$. Local finiteness implies that $J_x=\{i:x\in\overline{W_i}^{\,U}\}$ is finite and some neighbourhood meets no $W_i$ for $i\notin J_x$: first take a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many $W_i$, then avoid the closures of those not containing $x$. Closure containment from step 1.2 puts $x$ in every $U_{j(i)}$ for $i\in J_x$. The $c_i$ therefore have germs at $x$, all representing $s_x$. The stalk bijection [F6] makes their presheaf germs equal, so on one common smaller neighbourhood $N$ the finitely many cochains agree. Further shrink $N$ into a $W_{i_0}$ containing $x$ and away from all $W_i$ with $i\notin J_x$. Every simplex in $N$ is then assigned the value of $c_{i_0}$, independently of its chosen admissible index. Thus $c$ represents $s$ at every point of $U$. Every section over $U$ has a global representative; restricting that representative to any larger open set gives an extension. Hence every $\mathcal C^n$ is flasque. The canonical sheafification map $C^n(V;k)\to\mathcal C^n(V)$ is also onto for every open $V$.

(The flasque resolution.) The augmentation $k_X\to\mathcal C^0$ sends a locally constant function to the same function on points. By [F6], [F13], the cohomology of its stalk complex at $x$ is the colimit of the singular cohomology of neighbourhoods of $x$. Contractible open neighbourhoods are cofinal. A contraction and the cochain dual of [F5] identify their cohomology with that of a point. The ordinary singular cochain complex of a point has $k$ in every nonnegative degree, with differential $k\to k$ equal to zero in even degrees and the identity in odd degrees, because the boundary is the alternating sum of $n+1$ identical faces. Its cohomology is consequently $k$ in degree zero and zero otherwise. The augmentation induces the degree-zero stalk isomorphism, and all positive stalk cohomology vanishes. Therefore $k_X\to\mathcal C^0\to\mathcal C^1\to\cdots$ is exact. By steps 1.1 and 2.1 its terms are acyclic, and [F12] applies: the injective datum [F7] is defined on every successive kernel. Its section complex computes the $k$-linear derived cohomology. The same resolution consists of acyclic underlying abelian sheaves by step 1.1; applying [F12] with [F14] identifies its section cohomology also with the published abelian-sheaf convention.

(Identification with singular cohomology.) The canonical sheafification map $C^*(X;k)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)$ is surjective by step 2.1. Let $N^*$ be its kernel. A cochain lies in $N^*$ exactly when it vanishes on all simplices contained in some member of some open cover of $X$: a cochain has zero germ at $x$ exactly when it vanishes on all simplices of some neighbourhood of $x$ by [F6], and a cochain vanishing on the small simplices of a cover has zero germ everywhere, while conversely the neighbourhoods of all points form such a cover. For an open cover $\mathcal U$ let $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ be the subcomplex of cochains vanishing on the $\mathcal U$-small singular chains. By [F4] applied with coefficients in the field $k$, the inclusion of the small chain complex into all chains is a homology isomorphism, so the quotient chain complex is acyclic; over a field an acyclic chain complex of possibly infinite-dimensional spaces splits degreewise into its boundaries and a complementary subspace, and dualizing such a splitting shows that the Hom of the quotient into $k$ is acyclic. Since restriction of functions to the subcomplex of small chains is surjective, this dual complex is exactly $K^*_{\mathcal U}$; hence $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ is acyclic. The complexes $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ are directed by refinement, and their union is $N^*$. A cocycle in the union lies in one $K^*_{\mathcal U}$ and is a coboundary there, so $N^*$ is acyclic. The long exact sequence of the short exact sequence of cochain complexes $0\to N^*\to C^*(X;k)\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)\to0$ therefore identifies $H^*_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$ with the cohomology of $\Gamma(X,\mathcal C^*)$.

(Comparison and naturality.) Steps 3.1 and 3.2 identify $H^q(X,k_X)$ with $H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$ in all nonnegative degrees; both are zero in negative degrees. The comparison uses the canonical augmentation and sheafification map, not the choices used to prove surjectivity. For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$ between spaces satisfying the hypotheses, pullback of singular cochains on each open $V\subseteq Y$ gives cochains on $f^{-1}V$, commuting with differentials, restriction and the constant-sheaf augmentation. Sheafifying gives the same pullback morphism of resolutions. Thus the induced cohomology comparisons commute with pullback, proving naturality, in both the $k$-linear and abelian conventions compared in step 3.1.

(Open subspaces and finite-polyhedral consequences.) Every open subspace is metric and inherits the contractible-open basis, so the argument applies there. A nonempty contractible such space has the cohomology of a point by [F5]. For the remaining geometric claims, realize a finite simplicial complex in barycentric coordinates $(t_v)$ on its finite vertex set. If $x$ has support simplex $\sigma$, choose $0<\delta<\min_{v\in\sigma}t_v(x)$ and put $N_\delta(x)=\{y:|t_v(y)-t_v(x)|<\delta\ (v\in\sigma),\ \sum_{v\notin\sigma}t_v(y)<\delta\}$. These are open neighbourhoods and form a basis as $\delta\downarrow0$. Every carrier simplex of $y\in N_\delta(x)$ contains $\sigma$, so the segment from $y$ to $x$ stays in that carrier and satisfies the defining inequalities; these segments contract $N_\delta(x)$ to $x$. The open star of a simplex $\rho$ is $\{y:t_v(y)>0\ (v\in\rho)\}$. It is star-shaped toward the barycentre of $\rho$, since each carrier contains $\rho$ and the segment preserves these positive coordinates. Its nonempty intersection with a closed simplex $\tau$ requires $\rho\subseteq\tau$ and has the same contraction inside $\tau$. The intersections of the neighbourhoods $N_\delta(x)$ with these subspaces form contractible open neighbourhood bases: their contractions toward $x$ preserve the star's positive coordinates and membership in $\tau$. All these spaces inherit a metric from the finite coordinate space. Therefore their constant-sheaf cohomology is $k$ in degree zero and zero otherwise. An open star need not be convex in the whole realization; only these explicit contractions are used.

Then the abelian category $\mathrm{Mod}(\mathcal O_X)$ of $\mathcal O_X$-modules has enough injectives: every $\mathcal O_X$-module embeds into an injective $\mathcal O_X$-module, and the functorial injective embedding supplied by the Grothendieck injective-embedding theorem for Grothendieck categories supplies, by iteration of cokernels, one s

With supplied bounded-below injective replacements $j_X:X\to I_X$ (and DC or supplied homotopy extensions), $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal A)$ is an equivalence of triangulated categories.

In ZF, $$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$ DC here includes a prescribed initial point.
The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact.

A **triangulated subcategory** of $\mathcal T$ is a full additive subcategory closed under $[1]$ and $[-1]$ such that, with the inherited distinguished triangles, it satisfies the triangulated axioms.
Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let $x\in X$. Then there is a canonical isomorphism $$ (f^{-1}\mathcal G)_x\cong \mathcal G_{f(x)}.

Let $$ \cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots $$ be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. We use cochains as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], with $X[k]^n=X^{n+k}$ and $d_{X[k]}^n=(-1)^kd_X^{n+k}$. Thus $H^n(X[k])=H^{n+k}(X)$. The cochain category $K(\mathcal A)$ is the reindexed published homotopy category.

Let $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ be a morphism of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. The **kernel sheaf** is the subsheaf $$ \ker(\varphi)\subseteq \mathcal F $$ defined objectwise by $$ \ker(\varphi)(U):=\ker\!\bigl(\varphi_U:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal G(U)\bigr).

Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$ ([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as a topological space with its analytic topology ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and let $k$ be a field.

Let $S$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let $k$ be a field and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $S$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]]).

If $\mathcal A$ has enough injectives and $X^n=0$ for $n<a$, there is a termwise monic quasi-isomorphism $j:X\to I$ with each $I^n$ injective and $I^n=0$ for $n<a$. derivations.claim: (Setup.) A sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $X$ is an $\mathcal O_X$-module for the ringed space $(X,k_X)$ and conversely, and the stalk $k$ is a local ring, so $(X,k_X)$ is a locally ringed space with $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)=\mathrm{Mod}(k_X)$; this category is abelian, and $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is taken with the cochain conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], every Hom-set assertion being under its standing smallness hypothesis. In the second part, $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded and $\mathfrak S$-constructible.

(Extensions of local systems.) Let $0\to K\to E\xrightarrow{\pi}Q\to0$ be exact on any space $Y$, with $K,Q$ locally constant of finite rank. Near $y\in Y$ trivialize both, and let $e_1,\dots,e_q$ be the constant basis sections of $Q$. By [F6], their germs lift to $E_y$; represent these finitely many lifts by sections $t_i$ and shrink to one neighbourhood $N'$ where $\pi(t_i)=e_i$. For any open $W\subseteq N'$ and locally constant coefficients $a_i:W\to k$, define $s(\sum_i a_ie_i)=\sum_i a_it_i$ by gluing the ordinary scalar multiples on opens where all $a_i$ are constant. Locality makes this well defined and compatible with restriction, and $\pi s=\operatorname{id}$. Identifying $K$ with the kernel of $\pi$, the maps $(u,v)\mapsto u+s(v)$ and $e\mapsto(e-s\pi(e),\pi(e))$ are inverse sheaf morphisms between $K|_{N'}\oplus Q|_{N'}$ and $E|_{N'}$. Therefore $E$ is locally constant of finite rank. This uses finitely many lifts and no connected-neighbourhood hypothesis.

(Injective models.) By [F1] applied to $(X,k_X)$ every $k$-sheaf receives a specific injective resolution, and the category has enough injectives. AC supplies DC by [F3]. For each bounded-below complex, [F11] now supplies a bounded-below termwise injective replacement; the successive embeddings may be taken from the fixed embedding functor of [F1]. Thus the replacement hypothesis of [F2] is met for complexes as well as sheaves, and $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence. Hom groups between bounded complexes are therefore computed by homotopy classes of maps between their bounded-below injective replacements, using the fully faithful bounded embedding included in [F2].

(Shifts and isomorphisms.) Fix $\mathfrak S$ and let $A\in D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$. By [F7], $H^j(A[m])|_S=H^{j+m}(A)|_S$, so the cohomological support is reindexed and every restricted cohomology sheaf remains locally constant of finite rank. Isomorphic derived objects have isomorphic cohomology sheaves: the cohomology functors on complexes send quasi-isomorphisms to isomorphisms and therefore descend through localization. Hence the subcategory is closed under all shifts and isomorphisms.

(Cones on one stratum.) Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism in $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ and fix a stratum $S$. By [F6], inverse image to $S$ is exact, since its stalk maps are the original stalk maps. It preserves finite sums, differentials and shifts, hence cone complexes by [F7], and it preserves quasi-isomorphisms. Applying it to a bounded roof representing $f$ consequently gives a derived morphism and its cone triangle on $S$; no chain-map representative $A\to B$ is assumed. The long exact sequence [F4] yields $0\to\operatorname{coker}(f^j)\to H^j(C(f))|_S\to\ker(f^{j+1})\to0$, where $f^j:H^j(A)|_S\to H^j(B)|_S$. To check its end terms near $s\in S$, trivialize the finitely ranked source and target. The images of the finitely many constant basis sections have locally constant coordinate functions. Shrinking around $s$ makes these finitely many functions constant, without requiring a connected neighbourhood. The morphism is then a fixed matrix, whose kernel and cokernel are the constant sheaves on the corresponding finite-dimensional vector spaces, as follows either from locally constant functions or from [F8] stalkwise. Thus both end terms are locally constant of finite rank.

(Cone constructibility.) Steps 2.3 and 1.2 show that each $H^j(C(f))|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank. If $A$ and $B$ have cohomology only in finite intervals, their cone has cohomology only in the union of the interval for $B$ and the interval for $A$ shifted down one degree, by [F4]. A bounded roof also gives a bounded cone representative. Thus $C(f)\in D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$.

(Triangulated subcategory.) The zero complex belongs to the subcategory, and finite sums do too because their cohomology sheaves are the finite sums of the restricted local systems. By steps 2.2, 3.1 the full additive subcategory $D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ contains all isomorphs of its objects, is closed under shifts in both directions, and whenever $f$ is a morphism of the subcategory, a cone of $f$ lies in the subcategory. In a triangulated category the third object of any distinguished triangle with two objects in such a subcategory is isomorphic to a cone of a morphism between objects of the subcategory, so the subcategory is closed under the two-out-of-three operation; by the equivalent characterisation of [F5] it is a triangulated subcategory. If $A$ and $B$ with their cone are only asserted to be constructible with respect to one common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, the same argument applies with that stratification in place of $\mathfrak S$, giving the final sentence: their cone is bounded and constructible with respect to that common stratification. Only step 2.1 uses AC, exactly as declared in [A1].

citations.quote:
Let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety, i.e. a classical
algebraic variety over $\mathbb C$
([[def-classical-algebraic-prevariety-regular-maps-and-varieties]]), regarded as
a topological space with its analytic topology
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]), and
let $k$ be a field. Write $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ for the category of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces and $k$-linear morphisms
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is
an abelian category ([[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]), so its
bounded derived category $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is defined with the
conventions of [[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], under the
standing smallness hypothesis recorded there.

The category $D_c^b(X;k)$ is the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ consisting of the complexes $A$ satisfying:

1. $A$ is **cohomologically bounded**: $H^j(A)=0$ for $|j|$ sufficiently large;
   and
2. $A$ is **algebraically constructible**: there exists a finite smooth
   algebraic stratification with the frontier condition $\mathfrak S$ of $X$
   ([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]) such
   that for every stratum $S\in\mathfrak S$ and every integer $j$ the
   restriction $H^j(A)|_S$ is locally constant of finite rank
   ([[def-locally-constant-sheaf-of-finite-rank]]).

These are topological constructible sheaves, not coherent or quasi-coherent
sheaves. We use the shift convention of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]]: $H^j(A[m])=H^{j+m}(A)$. A
groupoid local system is identified with a locally constant sheaf only through
an explicit local comparison, which is not made here.

Constructibility is a condition on the cohomology sheaves of a complex, and it
is quantified existentially over finite smooth algebraic frontier
stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or
common-refinement theorem for stratifications is asserted by this definition.
Shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves cohomological boundedness
and shifts a witnessing stratification nowhere, so the class is closed under
shifts and under isomorphisms in $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$. No choice
principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological
space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space
$(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$
([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally
small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and
iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific
injective resolution
([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). These resolutions are
bounded-below injective replacements, so with the dependent choice supplied by
AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below
injective complexes model the bounded derived category:
$K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to
D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence, and morphisms of the bounded
derived category are computed by these replacements
([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let
$\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier
condition of $X$
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded
and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$
([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under
shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded
algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one
common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is
bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace
([[def-topological-space]]) with closed complement $Z=X\setminus U$, let
$i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of the subspace
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups
on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]]).
Write $\mathcal F|_U:=j^{-1}\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal F|_Z:=i^{-1}\mathcal F$ for
the restrictions ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]). Then:

1. the adjoint transpose of the identity of $\mathcal F|_U$ under the adjunction
   of [[thm-extension-by-zero-adjunction-exactness]] and the unit of the
   adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) fit into a short exact
   sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$
   $$0\to j_!(\mathcal F|_U)\to\mathcal F\to i_*(\mathcal F|_Z)\to0,$$
   where $j_!$ is extension by zero ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]]) and
   $i_*$ is the direct image ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]],
   [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]); exactness is that of
   [[def-exact-sequence-sheaves]];
2. if $\mathcal F=\mathbb Z_X$ is the constant sheaf with value $\mathbb Z$ on
   $X$, then $\mathcal F|_U$ is canonically isomorphic to the constant sheaf
   $\mathbb Z_U$ on $U$, so the sequence of clause 1 reads
   $0\to j_!(\mathbb Z_U)\to\mathbb Z_X\to i_*(\mathcal F|_Z)\to0$ up to that
   canonical isomorphism.

Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of a closed subset
$Z\subseteq X$ carrying the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), and
let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]])
whose stalks vanish off $Z$, that is $\mathcal G_x=0$ for every $x\in X\setminus Z$
([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]). Then the unit
$$\eta:\mathcal G\longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}\mathcal G$$
of the adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) between inverse image
and direct image ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]], [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]) is an
isomorphism of sheaves of abelian groups; equivalently
$\mathcal G\cong i_*(\mathcal G|_Z)$ under the identification
$\mathcal G|_Z=i^{-1}\mathcal G$ ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]).

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $f:C_\bullet\to D_\bullet$ be a chain map in an additive category. The
**mapping cone** of $f$ is the chain complex $\operatorname{Cone}(f)_\bullet$
whose degree-$n$ term is
$$\operatorname{Cone}(f)_n:=D_n\oplus C[1]_n=D_n\oplus C_{n-1},$$
and whose differential is
$$d_n^{\operatorname{Cone}(f)}(y,x):=(d_n^D(y)+f_{n-1}(x),-d_{n-1}^C(x)).$$

Thus $\operatorname{Cone}(f)$ is the direct sum of $D$ and the shift $C[1]$ as
a graded object, with the off-diagonal term given by $f$.

The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact. Every such triangle gives a long exact cohomology sequence $\cdots\to H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\to H^n(Z)\to H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: A sheaf on the point is its vector space of sections, and the point's unique stratification makes constructibility exactly finite-dimensional cohomology by [F1]. For a bounded complex $V$, choose complements $Z^n(V)=B^n(V)\oplus H^n$ and $V^n=Z^n(V)\oplus L^n$ using AC. The differential identifies $L^n$ with $B^{n+1}(V)$, so $V$ is the direct sum of the zero-differential complex $(H^n)$ and a contractible complex of pairs $L^n\xrightarrow{\sim}B^{n+1}(V)$. If all cohomology is finite-dimensional, $(H^n)$ is a bounded finite-dimensional representative, including the acyclic case where it is zero. Every vector space is injective under AC, because extending a basis splits every vector-space inclusion and extends every linear map from its subspace. Bounded complexes of vector spaces thus compute derived morphisms as homotopy classes by [F2], in both the finite-dimensional and full vector-space categories. For two finite-dimensional complexes these chain maps and homotopies are identical in both categories, proving full faithfulness as well as essential surjectivity. Hence $D_c^b(\operatorname{pt};k)\simeq D^b(k\text{-}\mathbf{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}})$.

On the point inverse and direct image of the identity are exact identity functors, and every section has compact support, so the proper-support functor is also the exact identity. Their derived functors are therefore identities. In the exceptional candidate of [[def-derived-operations-on-analytic-sheaves-over-locally-compact-spaces]], the fibre opens are only the point and the empty set; compact sections are exact, giving dimension bound $d=0$, and the constant sheaf $k$ is itself $c$-soft, so take $K=k[0]$. For a bounded finite-dimensional complex $B$ every term is injective over $k$, and the candidate has sections $\operatorname{Hom}_k^\bullet(k,B)=B$ on the point and zero on the empty set. Thus $f^!$ is the identity with its ordinary evaluation adjunction, and $\omega_{\operatorname{pt}}=a_{\operatorname{pt}}^!k=k[0]$. The ordinary-operations lemma [[lem-bounded-analytic-field-sheaves-have-derived-tensor-hom-and-pullback-pushforward-adjunctions]] identifies tensor and internal Hom with the finite signed complexes: $(A\otimes B)^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}A^p\otimes_kB^q$, with $d(a\otimes b)=d_Aa\otimes b+(-1)^pa\otimes d_Bb$, and $\mathcal Hom^n(A,B)=\prod_p\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^p,B^{p+n})$, with $d\varphi=d_B\varphi-(-1)^n\varphi d_A$. Their terms and amplitudes are finite, so they belong to the category identified in step 1.1. Here $f_*$ and $f_!$ in the Example denote their derived operations, which coincide with their exact underived functors in this case.

Apply [F3] to the constant sheaf $\mathcal F=k_{\mathbb C}$ on $X=\mathbb C$, with $U=\mathbb C^*$ and $Z=\{0\}$: the restriction $k_{\mathbb C}|_{\mathbb C^*}$ is the constant sheaf $k_{\mathbb C^*}$, the restriction to the closed point is $k$, and the sequence reads $0\to j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to0$, the terms being computed by [F5] for the extension by zero. Stalkwise the middle sheaf is exact: at $x\neq0$ the stalk of $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ is $k$ and the stalk of $i_*k$ is $0$, while at $0$ the first stalk is $0$ and the last is $k$; the quotient of $k_{\mathbb C}$ by $j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$ has no stalks off $\{0\}$, and by [F4] it is canonically the pushforward $i_*k$ of its restriction to the closed point. All maps are $k$-linear, since they are obtained from the canonical adjunction units of [F5] applied to $k$-sheaves.

In cochain grading, the cone $C$ of the map $g:k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k$ has $C^{-1}=k_{\mathbb C}$, $C^0=i_*k$ and differential $g$, by reindexing [F6]. Put $A=j_!k_{\mathbb C^*}$. The chain map $u:A[1]\to C$ given by the kernel inclusion in degree $-1$ is a quasi-isomorphism: step 2.2 gives $H^{-1}(C)=A$, $H^0(C)=0$, and $u$ induces the identity on the only possible nonzero cohomology. The cone triangle $k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to C\to k_{\mathbb C}[1]$ is distinguished by [F7]. Its signed inverse rotation and the quasi-isomorphism $-u:A[1]\to C$ give the distinguished triangle $A\to k_{\mathbb C}\to i_*k\to A[1]$ with the kernel inclusion as first arrow: the inverse rotation negates the projection $C[-1]\to k_{\mathbb C}$, cancelling the sign of $-u$. All three sheaves restrict to constant finite-rank sheaves (including rank zero) on each stratum of $\{\mathbb C^*,\{0\}\}$, so this localization triangle lies in $D_c^b(\mathbb C;k)$.

boundaries.evidence: The computed cases are the nonempty point and line; the underlying definitions cover the empty stratification vacuously, and no clause of the computation depends on an empty case.
The dualizing object is the field in degree zero and the cone of the line computation has its single cohomology sheaf in degree minus one; step 2.1 and step 3.1 record both conventions.
The point is the one-point case, computed in step 1.1, and the identity operations of step 2.1 constitute its six-operation computation.

No interval endpoints or limiting values occur; the inclusions are the exact open and closed inclusions of the line.
